title: Mechanisms and implications of drug-induced male reproductive toxicity and infertility: pharmacological agents, environmental toxicants, lifestyle factors, and emerging biomarkers for infertility, transgenerational effects, therapeutic interventions, and risk assessment through in vitro testicular models, high-throughput screening, and nanomaterial approaches
content:
Abstract
Male reproductive toxicity has emerged as a major global health concern due to increasing exposure to environmental pollutants, endocrine-disrupting chemicals, pesticides, and various pharmacological agents. Among plasticisers, di-(2-ethylhexyl) phthalate has received considerable attention for its ability to impair spermatogenesis, disrupt hormonal regulation, and reduce male fertility. Recent advances in computational toxicology—including network toxicology, molecular docking, and multi-omics analyses—have enabled the identification of key molecular targets and pathways involved in toxicant-induced reproductive dysfunction. Bioinformatic studies indicate that proteins such as prostaglandin-endoperoxide synthase 2, caspase-3, and oestrogen receptor-1 are central mediators of di-(2-ethylhexyl) phthalate-induced toxicity through mechanisms involving oxidative stress, apoptosis, inflammatory signalling, and endocrine disruption. Agricultural pesticides also contribute significantly to reproductive damage. Cypermethrin exposure disrupts testicular metabolic homeostasis by inhibiting the pentose phosphate pathway, reducing glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase activity, and impairing nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate production required for antioxidant defence. These metabolic disturbances promote oxidative stress and may compromise steroidogenesis and spermatogenesis. Emerging contaminants such as bisphenol S and hexafluoropropylene oxide dimer acid (GenX), as well as microplastics and nanoplastics, further intensify reproductive risk through oxidative imbalance and inflammatory responses. Drug-induced reproductive toxicity is another critical concern. Chemotherapeutic agents, particularly alkylating drugs, are strongly associated with gonadal damage and long-term infertility. Also, psychoactive medications, including selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, recreational substances, and developmental exposure to antidepressants, may impair sperm maturation, cause anejaculation, and compromised hormonal balance. Integrative analyses have also implicated phthalate metabolites such as monobenzyl phthalate in nonobstructive azoospermia through dysregulation of angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 and cytochrome P450 17A1 signalling pathways.
